rationale: A wins because it keeps the story shapes clean and refuses to make the facts do more work than they can bear. Its strongest line, “Figma's first big swing since the Adobe deal died is a bet on staying independent,” is a real follow-up angle with the IPO caveat handled honestly; B's “That's a different company than Adobe would have built” invents a counterfactual it cannot prove. B has useful material, but it keeps edging from inference into thesis, especially around production code, competitors, and investor meaning.
gaps_in_A: “first major move” is not stated in the update. Plausible, maybe, but a journalist will not let you smuggle it in without checking.
The independence angle depends on “an on-record Figma executive willing to address the post-Adobe strategy”; A knows this, but it means the best angle can collapse fast if Figma stays coy.
The handoff angle is strong, but “working front-end code” still needs a skeptical code-quality test before anyone pitches it as more than a demo.
The pricing angle says buyers can “do math” on 4M+ users and Fortune 500 usage, but it lacks seat-role clarity, so the budget impact is still speculative.
gaps_in_B: “Designers Can Ship Production Code” overclaims. The update says Make exports “working front-end code”; it does not say production-quality code or that designers can ship it.
“That's a different company than Adobe would have built” is strategy fan fiction unless Figma or a credible source says it.
“Vercel's v0, Framer, Webflow, Builder.io” are imported from outside the update. Useful market context, maybe, but not grounded enough for this blind exercise.
“The $25 'Make' Seat Tells You Exactly What Figma Is Selling Post-Adobe” oversells what pricing proves. A new paid seat is a monetization signal, not an X-ray of the whole post-Adobe strategy.
